summary: FireCase is an AI-powered, satellite-driven wildfire management platform that uses NASA Earth observation data, machine learning, and geospatial analysis to support wildfire prevention, early warning, emergency response, and environmental recovery. It integrates historical fire records, weather observations, and satellite-detected hotspots to identify unusual fire patterns, assess wildfire risks, and predict periods of increased hotspot activity. Its Random Forest model combined with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) achieved 95% overall accuracy, a 0.972 ROC-AUC, and successfully detected 18 out of 21 high-hotspot-activity days in its 2025 testing dataset, demonstrating its potential as an early-warning decision-support tool. Beyond prediction, FireCase aims to organize satellite fire detections into incident cases, prioritize emergencies based on fire intensity and proximity to communities and critical infrastructure, and monitor post-fire recovery through burned-area estimation and vegetation analysis. With accessible dashboards, interactive maps, and freely available NASA data, FireCase seeks to improve wildfire preparedness, strengthen evidence-based decision-making, optimize emergency response resources, and help communities manage environmental recovery more effectively.
details:
FireCase is an AI-powered, satellite-driven wildfire early warning, response, and recovery management platform designed to transform NASA Earth observation data into actionable, measurable insights for communities, emergency responders, firefighters, and land managers. Unlike traditional wildfire monitoring systems that primarily focus on detecting active fires, FireCase introduces an integrated approach that connects pre-fire risk assessment, active fire monitoring, and post-fire environmental recovery within a continuous case management framework. The platform combines NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), historical fire activity, national daily weather observations, machine learning, and geospatial analysis to identify unusual fire patterns, predict periods of elevated hotspot activity, and support evidence-based wildfire management decisions.

FireCase enables users to select geographical areas of interest through interactive maps, coordinate entry, or administrative boundaries. Its proposed monitoring capabilities include identifying satellite-detected hotspots, analyzing historical fire activity, calculating fire anomalies, and displaying location-specific risk indicators. Historical fire records from NASA's Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) support the development of a burning calendar that compares current fire activity against multi-year seasonal patterns. By combining satellite observations with environmental information, the platform aims to provide a more comprehensive assessment of wildfire conditions than hotspot visualization alone. Fire activity can be evaluated through measurable indicators such as the number of detected hotspots, percentage changes relative to historical averages, fire radiative power, predicted high-activity periods, and the geographical distribution of potentially affected areas.

A central data-driven component of FireCase is its developed Random Forest machine learning model integrated with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for predicting next-day high hotspot activity. The model was evaluated using national daily weather data combined with NASA FIRMS hotspot counts, with 2025 serving as the testing period. The dataset was organized into 406 training observations and 364 testing observations. High hotspot activity was defined using a threshold of 145.25, with the classification model distinguishing normal activity (Class 0) from high hotspot activity (Class 1). PCA reduced the predictor representation to four principal components while preserving 95.67% of the explained variance. This dimensionality reduction was incorporated to retain most of the information represented by the original predictors while simplifying the model's input structure.

The Random Forest and PCA model achieved an overall classification accuracy of 95.00% on the 364 testing observations, compared with a majority-class baseline accuracy of 94.23%. Although the improvement in accuracy was relatively small because normal-activity days dominated the dataset, the model demonstrated stronger discrimination through a Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.972 and a Precision-Recall Area Under the Curve (PR-AUC) of 0.772. These evaluation metrics provide a more informative assessment of performance under class imbalance than accuracy alone. The model's weighted-average precision, recall, and F1-score were approximately 0.96, 0.95, and 0.95, respectively, while its macro-average precision, recall, and F1-score were 0.75, 0.90, and 0.81. These results indicate strong overall classification performance while highlighting differences between the model's ability to identify normal and high-activity conditions.

The confusion matrix provides further evidence of the model's predictive capabilities. Among the 364 testing observations, 343 represented normal-activity days and 21 represented high-activity days. The model correctly classified 326 normal-activity days and successfully identified 18 of the 21 high-activity days. It generated 17 false-positive classifications and missed three actual high-activity days. For the high-activity class, the model achieved a recall of 85.71%, precision of 51.43%, and F1-score of approximately 0.64. This means that the model successfully identified approximately 86% of the high hotspot activity days in the testing period, although approximately 49% of its high-activity predictions were false alarms. These findings demonstrate the model's potential as an early-warning decision-support component while emphasizing the importance of balancing sensitivity against unnecessary alerts. The system is therefore intended to help prioritize monitoring and preparedness rather than independently confirm that a wildfire will occur.

The predictive model strengthens FireCase's proposed pre-fire monitoring functionality by providing quantitative estimates of elevated satellite hotspot activity before the following day's observations become available. By identifying 18 of the 21 high-activity days in the test dataset, the model demonstrates its ability to recognize patterns associated with increased national hotspot counts. This predictive capability can complement the platform's burning calendar and historical anomaly analysis by providing an additional indicator of potentially unusual fire conditions. However, its current evaluation concerns national-level next-day hotspot activity classification, rather than the precise prediction of individual wildfire ignition locations, fire spread, or community-level risk. Further geographic validation and operational testing are necessary before the model can support localized warning decisions.

During the active fire phase, FireCase is designed to transform NASA FIRMS satellite detections into structured incident cases containing geographical coordinates, observation timestamps, fire radiative power, and confidence information. Its proposed prioritization mechanism considers fire intensity and proximity to residential areas, forests, roads, power lines, and other critical infrastructure to help emergency responders identify incidents requiring closer attention. The platform also proposes distinguishing satellite detections from ground-verified fire reports through field verification and photographic evidence. Potential operational indicators include the number of detected hotspots, confirmed incidents, false alarms, high-priority cases, and the time between satellite detection and field verification. These capabilities are intended to improve situational awareness and support more efficient allocation of emergency personnel and resources. Unlike the Random Forest prediction model, these operational features are proposed components whose real-world performance has not yet been established by the provided evaluation results.

Following an active wildfire incident, FireCase is designed to transition the incident into a post-fire recovery case. The proposed recovery component incorporates satellite imagery and environmental observations to estimate burned areas, assess vegetation damage, and monitor landscape regeneration. NASA Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery, MODIS burned-area products, vegetation indices, precipitation observations, and Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) elevation data are identified as potential inputs for environmental monitoring. Post-fire assessment indicators include estimated burned area in hectares, vegetation recovery trends measured through the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), burn severity classifications, and locations that may be susceptible to secondary hazards such as erosion, landslides, and flash floods. These proposed functions aim to extend wildfire management beyond immediate fire containment and provide land managers with consistent information for restoration planning and long-term environmental assessment.

The project incorporates satellite data analytics, supervised machine learning, dimensionality reduction, and geospatial visualization within its technical approach. Its evaluated predictive component uses Random Forest classification combined with PCA, while the broader proposed architecture includes seasonal fire anomaly detection, spatial risk prioritization, fire spread modeling, satellite imagery analysis, and vegetation recovery monitoring. The use of four principal components retaining 95.67% of explained variance demonstrates the application of dimensionality reduction within the evaluated predictive workflow. The model's performance was assessed using a held-out 2025 testing dataset, a confusion matrix, classification metrics, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC. These evaluation methods enable the team to assess predictive effectiveness quantitatively and identify limitations arising from imbalanced wildfire activity observations.

FireCase's creativity lies in combining predictive satellite hotspot analytics with a continuous wildfire case management concept that connects early warning, emergency response, and environmental recovery. Its distinguishing feature is not simply the visualization of satellite fire detections, but the proposed integration of historical burning calendars, measurable anomaly indicators, validated machine learning predictions, risk-prioritized incident management, and post-fire environmental tracking. The model's 85.71% recall for high-activity days demonstrates a measurable predictive capability relevant to early warning, while its 51.43% positive-class precision reveals an important limitation that future development must address. By explicitly evaluating both successful detections and false alarms, FireCase emphasizes transparent, evidence-based prediction rather than relying solely on high overall classification accuracy.

The project's intended impact is to improve wildfire preparedness, strengthen data-driven decision-making, and support more efficient use of limited emergency response resources. The evaluated model identified 18 of 21 high hotspot activity days, providing preliminary evidence that satellite-derived historical activity and weather predictors can support next-day hotspot activity forecasting. In practice, such predictions could help monitoring organizations prioritize periods requiring closer observation. FireCase also aims to reduce dependence on costly proprietary monitoring infrastructure by using freely accessible NASA Earth observation data, although actual financial savings have not yet been measured. Future pilot evaluations can quantify operational benefits through detection-to-verification time, the number of unnecessary field investigations, response workload, monitoring coverage, and changes in resource utilization. These indicators would provide evidence of whether the platform improves operational efficiency beyond its demonstrated classification performance.

Accessibility and practical usability are important factors in the proposed system design. FireCase emphasizes interactive geographical selection, clear historical comparisons, understandable risk indicators, mobile-responsive dashboards, and role-specific information for emergency responders, firefighters, and land managers. Its proposed interface incorporates colorblind-accessible visualizations, text-based status labels, and exportable data to make satellite information understandable to users with different technical backgrounds. The platform also considers internet connectivity limitations, uncertainty in satellite observations, class imbalance in predictive modeling, the possibility of false-positive alerts, and the need for ground verification before operational action. These considerations are particularly relevant for local government units and resource-constrained communities that need accessible, scientifically grounded tools for wildfire management.

Ultimately, FireCase demonstrates how NASA Earth observation data can be combined with machine learning to support measurable improvements in wildfire monitoring and preparedness. Its Random Forest and PCA model achieved 95.00% overall accuracy, 0.972 ROC-AUC, and 0.772 PR-AUC on the reported 2025 test dataset, successfully detecting 18 of 21 high hotspot activity days while missing three. These findings provide a quantitative foundation for the project's predictive early-warning component and establish a baseline for future refinement. By extending this analytical capability into an integrated platform for fire monitoring, incident verification, prioritization, and environmental recovery, FireCase aims to bridge the gap between satellite science and practical disaster management. Its long-term vision is to transform publicly accessible Earth observation data into a reliable, interpretable, and cost-conscious decision-support resource that helps communities prepare earlier, respond more effectively, and monitor recovery more systematically.
